q: You are planning a short cut across the bay. One figure on the chart is underlined. What does it tell you?
a: A rock or bank dries 1.2 m above datum
o: There is 1.2 m of water over it at datum
There is 12 m of water — the line is a decimal
There is 1.2 m more water than the chart shows
why: An underlined sounding is a drying height: it stands that much above chart datum. Keep well clear.

fig.note: Depths in metres below chart datum

q: You have drawn today's leg on the paper chart and spanned it with dividers. Where do you read off the distance in miles?
a: On the latitude scale at the side, level with the leg
o: On the longitude scale along the top or bottom
On the outer ring of the compass rose
On the kilometre scale bar under the title
why: One minute of latitude is one nautical mile; minutes of longitude shrink as you go north.

q: You have a 1:50 000 chart of the area and a 1:10 000 harbour plan in the pilot book. Which do you use to pick your way into the harbour?
a: The 1:10 000 plan — larger scale, more detail
o: The 1:50 000 chart — bigger number, more detail
Either — same detail, only drawn at another size
Neither — only the plotter shows harbour detail
why: 1:10 000 is a larger scale than 1:50 000: a smaller area drawn in more detail.

q: You are coming in to this town quay to berth stern-to. Which spot do you ask for?
a: C — 4.0 m leaves water under the keel
o: A — the root of the quay is most sheltered
B — 2.0 m, the tide will add the rest
Any — depths on a plan are only a guide
why: Pick a berth deeper than your draft, with a margin; the Med tide adds almost nothing.

fig.note: Depths in metres alongside the quay

q: You want a swim stop before the afternoon leg. What is the latest time you can leave the swim stop?
why: 12 M at 6 kn takes 2 hours; with an hour in hand you arrive at 16:00, so leave by 14:00.

fig.title: Lead crew briefing
lines: Your speed under engine: about 6 kn
Be in by 17:00 — keep an hour in hand

q: The lead crew wants every boat at the lunch stop, 14 miles away, by 13:00. You leave at 09:30. What average speed do you need?
o: 3.5 knots
4.5 knots
5 knots
why: 09:30 to 13:00 is 3.5 hours; 14 M ÷ 3.5 h = 4 knots.

q: You have drawn the course to the next headland on the chart. What do you steer by the compass?
why: True to magnetic: subtract easterly variation — 140° − 4° = 136°.

q: You take this bearing of a lighthouse with the hand-bearing compass. Which true bearing do you draw on the chart?
why: Magnetic to true: add easterly variation — 030° + 5° = 035°.

q: You are entering harbour on a leading line. The rear beacon has moved a little to the right of the front one. What do you do?
a: Alter to port until they are in line again
o: Alter to starboard until they are in line again
Hold course — they will line up as you close
Steer straight for the rear beacon instead
why: Rear mark open to the right of the front means you are right of the line: come back to port.

q: The pilot book says: 'Enter with the chapel in line with the white house, 320°.' Why follow the transit rather than steer 320° on the compass?
a: It shows at once if wind or current set you off
o: It allows for variation, so no sums are needed
It still works when the visibility closes in
It also tells you how far off the entrance you are
why: A transit is a line on the ground: if the marks open, you are off it, whatever your heading.

q: You plan to spend the night at anchor here. How much water do you plan on?
a: About 3 m — the charted depth, give or take a little
o: About 1.5 m — half the charted depth at low water
Under 1.9 m — you will touch at low water
About 6 m — double the charted depth at high water
why: Med tides are tiny and chart datum is near the lowest level, so the charted depth is about what you get.

fig.title: Ionian anchorage
lines: Pilot book: tidal range about 0.3 m

q: You are motoring along the coast in clear weather. What do you make of this?
a: The chart on the plotter is offset — trust your eyes
o: The headland is nearer than it looks — trust the plotter
The sounder is faulty — the plotter is always right
The GPS has lost its fix — stop the boat at once
why: Electronic charts can be offset by tens or hundreds of metres; what you see and the sounder come first.

fig.title: Plotter vs. what you see
lines: Plotter: your boat drawn on the land
Headland about 300 m off to port

q: Today's route takes you through a narrow pass between an island and a reef. The plotter is working well. How do you take the pass?
a: Follow the plotter, checking it against marks and depth
o: Zoom the plotter right in and follow its line exactly
Engage the autopilot on the plotter's route
Trust the GPS alone — it is accurate to a few metres
why: The GPS is good, but the chart under it may not be: confirm with transits, bearings and the sounder.

q: You are at anchor at 38°31'N. The next anchorage is due north at 38°43'N. How long does it take at 6 knots?
o: 12 minutes
1 hour 12 minutes
3 hours
why: 12 minutes of latitude = 12 M; 12 M ÷ 6 kn = 2 hours.

q: You check the route you drew for this afternoon against the chart. What do you do?
a: Redraw the leg to pass clear of the 1.8 m patch
o: Go as drawn — 1.8 m is near enough your draft
Go as drawn, but slow down over the patch
Go as drawn — the tide will give you more water
why: The track crosses a sounding shallower than your draft; plan every leg clear of it with a margin.

q: You enter the lead crew's lunch-stop waypoint into the plotter and press 'Go to'. What must you do before following the line?
a: Check the straight line on the chart for land and shoals
o: Nothing — the plotter steers round any danger
Check only that the waypoint name is right
Set the autopilot first so you hold the line
why: 'Go to' draws a straight line, and it will cross headlands, rocks and shallows if they are in the way.

q: You are motoring along this coast toward the headland. The pilot book gives the clearing bearing shown. What do you do?
a: Turn offshore until the bearing drops below 070°
o: Hold on — over 070° means you are well clear
Turn inshore until the bearing reads 070°
Hold course and check again at the headland
why: 078° is on the wrong side of the clearing line, toward the rocks: turn away until it is below 070°.

q: When do you expect to arrive in the evening harbour?

fig.title: Today's plan
lines: Leg 1: 9 M at 6 kn to the lunch bay
Leg 2: 6 M at 4 kn under sail

q: You are motoring in exactly on the leading line from the pilot book. What does the steering compass tell you?
a: It is right — 312° true is 307° magnetic
o: It reads 5° low — have it checked
You are 5° off the line — alter course
The pilot book's line is 5° wrong
why: Easterly variation is subtracted: 312° − 5° = 307°M, so the compass has no deviation on this heading.

q: You want to put your position on the paper chart. What latitude do you plot?
